title: setContext / getContext Component Hierarchy Scopes
prerequisites: Understanding of props vs shared state

progressiveExplaining.eli5: A family has a shared household notebook. The grandparents write the household rules in the notebook, and any child or grandchild in the same house can open it and read the rules — but only people inside the house. Neighbors and guests can't see it. If a grandchild moves to a different house, they get that house's notebook instead. The notebook is shared down the family tree, not across the whole street. That's how shared household knowledge works: it flows down through the nested rooms of one house only.
progressiveExplaining.junior: setContext(key, value) stores a value for the current component; getContext(key) retrieves the nearest value set by an ancestor. Call them during component initialization: setContext('theme', theme); then in a descendant: const theme = getContext('theme');. The key can be a string, symbol, or object (often a Symbol or an object with an id to avoid collisions). Use context for: providing services/config to descendants without prop drilling, per-component-instance singletons, and library APIs (like SvelteKit's page store). Context is not reactive by itself — pass a $state value or store to share reactivity.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, the context API is a per-component-instance key-value store: setContext associates a value with the current component's instance scope, and getContext walks up the component tree (the instance's parent chain) to find the first ancestor that set that key. It is component-hierarchy-scoped, unlike module-level singletons, so different subtrees can have different values. It is the idiomatic Svelte dependency-injection mechanism. Because it is non-reactive (a plain lookup), you should store reactive values (a $state reference, a store, or a writable) and let reactivity flow through that value, not through context itself.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: Each component instance has an internal context map (a Map keyed by the context key). setContext writes into the current instance's map; getContext checks the current instance's map, then walks up via the instance's parent reference (the component tree), returning the first match or undefined. This is a simple prototype-chain-like lookup over the instance tree, implemented as a plain per-instance Map in the runtime. SvelteKit and libraries use this to pass 'page', 'navigate', etc. down the tree. Context values are captured at component init; if you call getContext outside component initialization, it throws (no current instance).

rosettaStone.react: React's Context.Provider/useContext is the analogue, though it's implemented via the fiber tree and re-renders consumers.
rosettaStone.angular: Angular DI (providers + inject) provides the same hierarchy-scoped service sharing.
rosettaStone.vue: Vue's provide()/inject() is the direct equivalent.

codeComparison.title: Prop drilling vs setContext/getContext
codeComparison.summary: Threading the same value through many props couples components and bloats signatures; context shares it down the subtree without prop wiring.

fullFile.code:
<!-- ❌ OLD: Prop drilling. Every level between the source and the
     consumer must declare and forward the prop, even if the middle
     components never use it. Adding a value means touching every
     component in the chain. -->
<script>
  import Parent from './Parent.svelte';
  let theme = $state('light');
</script>

<Parent theme={theme} /> <!-- ❌ OLD: must forward -->

<!-- Parent.svelte must do: let { theme } = $props(); then forward it:
     <Child theme={theme} />
     Child.svelte then receives it. Every hop is boilerplate, and any
     component that forgets to forward breaks the chain silently. -->

modernOrGood.label: setContext/getContext

fullFile.code:
<!-- ✅ NEW: Context flows down the component tree without props. -->
<script>
  import Child from './Child.svelte';
  let theme = $state('light'); // ✅ NEW: reactive state value

  // ✅ NEW: store the reactive reference in context once
  setContext('theme', theme);
</script>

<Child /> <!-- ✅ NEW: no prop forwarding needed -->

<!-- Deep in the tree (any descendant):
  <script>
    import { getContext } from 'svelte';
    // ✅ NEW: reads the nearest ancestor's value
    const theme = getContext('theme');
    $effect(() => console.log('theme is', theme)); // reactive via the $state ref
  </script>
  The context holds the state reference, so reactivity flows through it. -->

interviewGotchas.question: Is context reactive, and how do you share reactive values through it correctly?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests a common misconception — interviewers want to confirm you know setContext is a plain lookup, and that reactivity comes from the VALUE you store, not from context itself.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Context itself is non-reactive: setContext writes a value into a Map, and getContext returns whatever was stored — it does not track reads or re-deliver on change. If you set a primitive (setContext('theme', 'light')) and later change it, descendants that already called getContext keep the old value. To share reactive state, store a reactive container: a $state variable (setContext('theme', themeState)), a Svelte store, or a writable. Then descendants read the container and subscribe/react to its changes through the normal reactive mechanisms (reading the $state in templates/effects, or the store's $ syntax). The pattern 'context carries the reference, reactivity lives in the value' is the correct mental model.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'setContext makes the value reactive'. It only shares the reference at init time. Another trap: calling setContext/getContext outside component initialization — getContext outside init throws, and calling setContext after the tree has read it has no retroactive effect. Candidates who explain the reference-carrying pattern show real understanding.

interviewGotchas.question: How does getContext resolve values when multiple ancestors set the same key, and how is this different from a module singleton?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This probes the scoping semantics — the nearest-ancestor lookup and per-subtree isolation that distinguish context from global singletons.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: getContext starts at the current component instance and walks UP the component tree (parent, grandparent, ...), returning the first instance whose context map contains the key. So if a parent sets 'theme' and a grandparent also sets 'theme', the child gets the parent's value — nearest ancestor wins. This per-tree resolution means two sibling subtrees can each provide different values for the same key without conflict. Contrast with a module-level singleton (an exported variable), which is shared globally across the whole app — no scoping, no per-subtree variation, and it cannot be provided differently per instance. Context is the hierarchical, instance-scoped alternative, which is why component libraries use it for per-component configuration.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'context is like a global store'. It is scoped to the component subtree and resolved nearest-first. Another trap: assuming keys must be unique strings — string keys can collide across libraries, so Symbol or object keys are recommended to avoid accidental collisions. Candidates who describe the ancestor walk and the collision-avoidance keying show real depth.
